items.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: “Well that doesn’t look like Rembrandt,” or “It doesn’t look like Monet,”

ctx.x: Well I mean you know, so you used the magic word “acceptable.” That depends. Because it’s the same — at least in Western music it’s the same twelve tones. It’s still the same twelve tones. But what you could do with them is a lot different than it was hundreds of years ago of course. So nothing has changed, the only thing that has changed is people doing what they want to do. So really when you say “wrong” note or “right” note, it’s almost according to what? You know according to what? So if you say a system of…

“Well that doesn’t look like Rembrandt,” or “It doesn’t look like Monet,” it looks like — and then another person says, “Yeah but look how this yellow drips down, it mixes with this red and I did it with no kind of egoic intent at all, I just did it in gravity and do it, and who said art isn’t that? And what it looks like and whatever you think it is is what’s still art. So you can get into all these banter, these intellectual arguments, but for me at this point, a wrong note, I don’t know if there is such a…

Well I’ve struggled to find a better word than “wrong.” And most people answer well what’s your intent or what did you do to justify, and I just want to insert something about what you were talking about with the bucket of paint, that in 1998 you said to me, “Almost anything that human beings that alter God or nature can be art.”
